newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Balkan air carriers fear more open skies.
newsitem.headline: Balkan air carriers fear more open skies.

text.p: Balkan air carriers must join forces to proptect themselves against any negative consequences of global liberalisation of air transport, Balkan air carriers said on Wednesday.

Opening Balkan skies to more European competition could jeopardize small national air carriers in the region, Dimitris Tsatsalides, deputy president of the Greek OSPA Olympic Airlines trade union, told a meeting of regional air traffic trade unions.
Trade unions said the Balkan market of 50-60 million people represented big enough space for regional airlines, but any competition by the big air carriers would squeeze them from their own markets.

"National air carriers from the Balkans need to avoid (airlines)...such as Lufthansa and British Airways and to cooperate and block them, because if they succeed, national air carriers will cease to exist," Tsatsalides said.

The Second Balkan Conference of Air Transport Trade Unions opened in Belgrade, attracting air transport trade union representatives from Greece, Slovenia, Romania, Moldova, Macedonia and Yugoslavia. The first conference was held last May in Thessaloniki.
Trade unions gathered for a two-day meeting to discuss air transport liberalisation, air carriers privatisation and implications on their employees' social status.

"Liberalisation is a long-term, global process which big companies impose on small ones. The Balkan market is an interesting area for wide and open activities," Yugoslav Airlines (JAT) managing director Zika Petrovic said.

Petrovic insisted Balkan air carriers could not avoid liberalisation and cautioned the process would very quickly reflect on local companies, which operated in the region where the industry's turnover stood between $4 and $4.5 billion a year and where air traffic was seen expanding further.
"We are a part of Europe but with different economic and air traffic levels," he said.
President of the Serbian Air Traffic And Aviation Workers' Trade Union Rade Savic said trade unions could not accept the industry's globalisation unconditionally.

"In a global world economy, we cannot agree to adjust through reducing the number of workers or cutting wages. Profit, prosperity and contact with the first neighbours is a unique economic formula. Trade unions support changes, but only if agreed with workers' representatives," Savic said. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
